summary:
Martinique is an overseas department of France and stands under the French national framework in full: Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the island, so the identity documents, criminal law, anti-discrimination provisions and marriage regime a visitor would rely on are national law operating locally. A trans visitor is subject to the same substantive rules as in metropolitan France, administered through the department's own courts, administrative services and registry offices, and no island-specific procedure or exemption applies.

Martinique's correctional establishments are French prisons, so the national placement rules and the national detention watchdog's findings on transgender detainees apply to them by virtue of being French places of deprivation of liberty; no rule specific to the department governs placement, isolation or safety there. The watchdog's on-site interviews were conducted at establishments outside the department, so that finding rests on referrals and inspections elsewhere while still binding Martinique's prisons.

Same-sex conduct has been lawful in Martinique since 1815. The 2013 marriage-equality law applies in the department, discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been prohibited in goods and services since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2) and in employment since 2008 (Labour Code article L1132-1), and gender-identity discrimination has been prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with the term "sexual identity" replaced by "gender identity" in 2016.

Community infrastructure operates on the island. JM Concept 972 runs information, meetings and services for Martinique's LGBT community, and LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.
tangentialFactors:
The support network that names Martinique sits alongside organisations listed for the wider group of overseas departments. A visitor moving between these French Caribbean departments encounters the same national legal rules and a community network that crosses administrative borders.

Conditions inside the department's prisons are documented through national rather than island sources: inspections and press reporting on transgender detainees in French custody were produced for the national prison estate as a whole, and Martinique's establishments fall within their scope because they are French prisons.

The Rights in Exile listing places Martinique inside a country-by-country directory of sexual orientation and gender identity resources, so some of the legal material indexed under the entry concerns France as a whole rather than the department alone.
localsOnly:
Residents' legal business is handled locally: the department's courts, registry offices and administrative services process identity documents, marriage and discrimination complaints under national rules, with no island-specific variant of the procedure.

JM Concept 972 provides information, meetings and services to Martinique's LGBT community and runs private parties and garden parties, with 2025 events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September, supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters.

The Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Martinique page gathers local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts alongside the provisions in force on the island; the case law and expert material it indexes is the locally grounded record available to residents and to anyone preparing a claim about the department.
outOfScopeNotes:
No figures specific to Martinique on anti-trans violence, and no enforcement record specific to the island, were located in the sources consulted. National hate-crime statistics exist but cover France as a whole and are documented at national level rather than as findings about the department.

The resource page records 1815 as the date same-sex conduct was decriminalised in the department; it gives no account of enforcement or of local practice in the intervening period.

Details of legal gender recognition procedure, gender-affirming care provision and the status of youth transition care are national matters under the framework in force in the department; they are not sourced here as island-specific findings.
